# Homographies {#sec-homography}

## Introduction

In @sec-geometry_homogeneous we discussed several types of
geometric transformations of two-dimensional (2D) images: translations,
rotations, skewing, scalings, and we saw that all could be modeled as
the product between the coordinates of a point in the input image
described using homogeneous coordinates and a $3 \times 3$ matrix. Now
that we have discussed camera models, we are well equipped to present a
more general geometric image transformation that opens the door to many
applications: the homography.

As we discussed in the previous @sec-stereo_vision, if we capture a scene with two cameras
from different viewpoints, corresponding points across both images are
constrained by the epipolar constrain. In general, there is not a simple
geometric transformation that maps pixels from one image into the pixels
of the other image. To find that mapping we will need to know the
three-dimensional (3D) location of each point as well as the relative
camera translation and rotation between both images.

However, there are a few scenarios where we can find a simple
transformation that allows warping one image into another image
corresponding to a new camera location without requiring knowing the 3D
scene structure: this will happen when the scene is planar (as in
@fig-illustration_homography) or when the two cameras are related just
by a rotation (@fig-rotation_homography). In those two cases the
coordinates of corresponding points across the two images are related by
a **homography**.


:::{#fig-illustration_homography layout-ncol="2"}
![](figures/homography/IMG_7801_crop.jpg){width="45%"}

![](figures/homography/IMG_7802_crop.jpg){width="48%"}

These two images are (approximately) related by an homography.
:::

elements: Optical center (black sphere at the origin)
Coordinate axes at the origin labeled X, Y, and Z
Camera 1 image plane: green semi-transparent rectangle
Camera 2 image plane: red semi-transparent rectangle (rotated around the optical center)
Rotation arc 'R' showing the rotation from Camera 1 to Camera 2
Two black projection rays originating from the optical center, piercing both the green and red image planes
Intersection point markers (small yellow dots) on both planes for each projection ray
A grid texture projected on both planes to visually demonstrate the homographic distortion

interactions.label: Rotation (R)
interactions.teaches: How the angle of rotation between the two cameras alters the homography mapping and plane intersection

interactions.label: Ray Sweep
interactions.teaches: Demonstrates the point-to-point correspondence as the optical ray sweeps across the overlapping fields of view

demo_steps.title: Shared Projection Center
demo_steps.narration: Notice that both Camera 1 (green) and Camera 2 (red) share the exact same optical center (the black origin sphere). Because there is no translation between them, there is no depth parallax.

demo_steps.title: Point-to-Point Mapping
demo_steps.narration: As you sweep the projection ray, observe how a single line from the optical center pierces both planes. This creates a direct, unique mapping from every pixel in Camera 1 to a pixel in Camera 2.

demo_steps.title: Varying the Camera Rotation
demo_steps.narration: Adjusting the rotation angle alters the homography. Notice how the grid pattern on the red plane warps dynamically relative to the green plane, illustrating the projective transformation mathematically described by the homography matrix H.

(2) This receding angle suggests the camera is placed broadside-left, looking at an azimuth of roughly -40 degrees relative to the plane normal.
